feedback: If a learner says it is 'a different Moon each night' or that clouds cover part of it, point back to the ordered diary strip: it is the same Moon, and the shape changes gradually and repeats. Clouds can hide part of the Moon on some nights, but the slowly changing shape seen on clear nights is not made by clouds.
If a learner is surprised to see the Moon in daytime, affirm the real sighting — the Moon rises and sets at different times, so it is sometimes up in daylight.
Praise predictions that use the recorded pattern (e.g. 'it has been getting fatter, so next it will be fatter still, until it is full and then starts getting thinner') rather than guesses.
activities.intendedInsight: The Moon's shape changes in a dependable, repeating cycle over about a month, so you can use past observations to predict what comes next — and the Moon is sometimes visible by day, not only at night.
learnerActions: Whenever the Moon can be seen in a clear sky (often in the evening, but on some nights it is not up at a child's evening viewing time or cannot be seen at all), draw the shape of the Moon you can see, dating each drawing, and mark 'not seen' on other nights.
Keep the drawings in order on a strip or class calendar so the sequence builds up over about a month.
After a week or two, look back at the pattern and PREDICT: draw what you think the Moon will look like in a few nights.
Check your prediction against the next real observation and talk about whether the shape is fattening or thinning.
Watch for and record any time you spot the Moon in the daytime too.
activities.title: Month-long Moon-shape diary

feedback: Always record that the Sun APPEARS to move/rise/set — accept and praise the observed pattern without yet claiming the Sun itself travels; the cause (Earth's rotation) comes later.
Reinforce safe observation: positions are read from the shadow stick's shadow, never by looking at the Sun.
If a learner puts stars only in 'night', accept it for the sort but add that the stars are still there in the day, just hidden by the bright sky.
Reinforce correct predictions by linking them to the earlier observations the learner made.
activities.intendedInsight: The Sun follows the same daily rising-arcing-setting pattern (only shifting slowly over the seasons), so its apparent position at a given time is predictable; the Sun is seen by day and the stars by night, while the Moon can be seen in either.
learnerActions: At morning, midday and afternoon on the same day, record where the Sun appears — safely and indirectly, by marking the shadow cast by a fixed stick or object (a shadow stick); the Sun is on the opposite side of the stick from its shadow. NEVER look at or stare directly at the Sun.

Compare the three recorded positions and describe the path: the Sun appears to climb higher towards midday (shortest shadow) and then get lower in the afternoon, fitting the pattern of rising on one side and setting on the other.
Predict where the Sun will appear at lunchtime (or another time), then check by reading the shadow again — not by looking at the Sun.
Sort a set of sky objects/pictures into 'seen by day', 'seen by night', and 'sometimes both' (Sun by day; stars by night; Moon sometimes in both).
activities.title: Mark the Sun's daily path

feedback: The diagnostic is the pre-observation reason: a child who predicts 'it goes off' may be holding the stars-disappear idea — check by asking about the stars directly.

If a learner explains daytime invisibility by the stars being absent, respond: the stars are still there; the daytime sky is simply too bright to see them — like a small dim light that is hard to see in a brightly-lit room.
Target answer to voice and reinforce: 'You can't see the stars in the daytime because the sky is too bright — the Sun's light washes them out — but the stars are still there all along.'
activities.intendedInsight: A dim light is still on even when a much brighter light washes it out — just as the stars are still present in the daytime but hidden by the bright, Sun-lit sky.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, turn on a small dim LED night-light.
Before anything changes, PREDICT with a reason: when all the big room lights come on, will the little light still be shining or will it go off? Commit to your answer out loud.
Turn on all the big lights and watch — the little light becomes much harder to see and may seem to vanish, even though it is still on.
Dim the room again and watch it reappear.
Say what this shows about why we can't see the stars in the daytime.
activities.title: Dim-light predict-observe-explain (stars hidden by day)

feedback: Full understanding: describes the patterns AND explains stars are still present by day but hidden by the bright sky, and knows the Moon cycles over about a month and is sometimes visible by day.
Partial: describes the patterns but explains star-invisibility by 'they're not there' rather than 'the sky is too bright' — reteach with the dim-light demo.
Gap: thinks stars and Moon appear and disappear with no sense of a repeating pattern — return to the diary and Sun-path observations.
activities.intendedInsight: Demonstrate that you can describe and predict the sky patterns and explain that daytime stars are hidden, not gone.
learnerActions: Put a scrambled set of Moon-phase pictures back into the correct order.
Given the last few Moon shapes in order, choose which shape comes next.
Sort sky objects into day-sky vs night-sky (with 'sometimes both' available for the Moon).
Answer and give a reason: in the daytime, can you see the stars? Why do you think that is?
activities.title: Pattern check: sequence and sort
